'''Carl Louis Ferdinand von Lindemann''' (12 April 1852 &ndash; 6 March 1939) was a German [[mathematician]] who proved in 1882 that [[pi|{{pi}}]] (pi) is a [[transcendental number]], meaning it is not a [[Polynomial#Solving polynomial equations|root]] of any nonzero [[polynomial]] with [[rational number|rational]] [[coefficient]]s.

== Life and education ==
Lindemann was born in [[Hanover]], the capital of the [[Kingdom of Hanover]]. His father, Ferdinand Lindemann, taught modern languages at a [[gymnasium (school)|gymnasium]] in Hanover. His mother, Emilie Crusius, was the daughter of the gymnasium's headmaster. The family later moved to [[Schwerin]], where young Ferdinand attended school.

He [[Research|studied]] mathematics at the [[University of Göttingen]], the [[University of Erlangen–Nuremberg|University of Erlangen]], and the [[Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München]]. At the University of Erlangen, he received a doctorate, supervised by [[Felix Klein]],<ref name="Klein" /> on [[non-Euclidean geometry]]. Lindemann subsequently taught in [[Würzburg]] and at the [[University of Freiburg]]. During his time in Freiburg, Lindemann devised his proof that {{pi}} is a transcendental number (see the [[Lindemann–Weierstrass theorem]]). After his time in Freiburg, Lindemann transferred to the [[University of Königsberg]]. While a professor in [[Königsberg]], Lindemann acted as supervisor for the doctoral theses of the mathematicians [[David Hilbert]], [[Hermann Minkowski]], and [[Arnold Sommerfeld]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ferdinand von Lindemann - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Lindemann/ |access-date=2022-08-06 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref>

== Transcendence proof ==
In 1882, Lindemann published the result for which he is best known, the [[Transcendental number|transcendence]] of [[pi|{{pi}}]].<ref>{{cite journal | last=Lindemann | first=F. | title=Ueber die Zahl {{pi}}*) | journal=[[Mathematische Annalen]] | volume=20 | issue=2 | date=1882 | issn=0025-5831 | doi=10.1007/BF01446522 | pages=213–225 | url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF01446522 | language=de | access-date=2026-04-12}}</ref>  His methods were similar to those used nine years earlier by [[Charles Hermite]] to show that ''[[E (mathematical constant)|e]]'', the base of [[natural logarithm]]s, is transcendental, and the works of [[Joseph Liouville]] from the 1840s establishing the existence of transcendental numbers.<ref name=":3">{{cite book |last=Dunham |first=William |author-link=William Dunham (mathematician) |title=The Calculus Gallery |publisher=Princeton University Press |year=2005 |isbn=978-0-691-13626-4 |page=}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=127}} Before the publication of Lindemann's proof, [[Johann Heinrich Lambert]] had already [[Proof that pi is irrational#Lambert's proof|shown that {{pi}} is irrational in 1768]].<ref name=":3" />{{Reference page|page=119}}
